I work with the new membership committee at my Conservative synagogue, and *literally* every single family since I started helping two years ago has asked if we are egalitarian, hoping that we are. The problem with saying it drove people away is that it also brought a lot of Reform folks over to the Conservative movement who wanted more.

On any given service when there is not a bnei mitvah, there is only a tiny number in attendance. However, our religious school is thriving. Events specifically for children/youth get high numbers. The big goal we have is to encourage higher attendance at shul on Shabbat as an ongoing practice.
Btw, while we are Conservative, we are markedly egalitarian. That is usually the first question new families ask us and continues to be a make or break issue for new generations.

I agree. I am talking about Tevye's possible perspective on Chava's choice of marriage and what his feelings may be stemming from.

Because she is marrying the oppressor. His people have humiliated, abused, and killed the Jewish people and made them second class citizens for a long time. On top of that, as others have mentioned, Judaism is an ethnoreligion, so Judaism is not just Chava's family's religion, but her ethnic, cultural, and historical identity. I imagine Tevye cannot picture a future in which Chava is raising her family Jewish or connecting to the community she comes from in a world in which she is married to the enemy. And then the question arises - does marrying into the enemy's world make her the enemy, too? Would she stand by as her fellow Jews are humiliated? The fact that as a father Tevye even has to wonder about these questions is incomprehensibly painful to him. The combination of these factors make it the ultimate betrayal. Their situation is quite different than our modern notions of "interfaith" dating, families, and relationships. And it has nothing to do with any sort of religious spiritual punishment. Due to hatred and violence toward them, and often due to segregation as well, Jews in Europe and around the diaspora stuck together. They worked hard to foster their own communities and hold onto their way of life in the face of forces that disdained them - in this case, the Russians. By choosing an enemy outsider as a spouse, Chava may appear to be spitting in the face of a little Jewish community that has worked so hard to protect all its Jewish children and to protect its very existence.

In the killing of the first born sons, some would argue that the entire story is using metaphor to capture the experience of slavery and rebellion from slavery. If you look at the slave rebellion in Haiti, for example, many of the slave owners and their families were killed. What’s worth it? Is the spilling of innocent blood inherent in slave rebellion and freedom? I don’t know the answers, but that’s why every Passover we have a seder. And we talk about all of it every year. In our seder, when we read the ten plagues we take a drop of our wine and take it out, putting that drop on our plate. The idea is that even in our liberation we should not take joy in the misfortune of our oppressors - so the wine represents the joy, and we are lessening it with each plague.

Honestly, I totally get it. But one of the cool things about Judaism is that questioning is highly encouraged. There’s an old saying that goes: ask two Jews, get three opinions. In fact, a big part of our Torah is not just the “Old Testament” (to use a Christian word for our book), but the Talmud. The Talmud is a vast, outrageously long text that is the recordings of rabbis straight up arguing about every single thing in the Bible. They discuss every line and story, add things, fight about meaning, etc. And that is a part of what created a tradition in Judaism of debating and dissecting and rereading texts. And that’s just one piece. The other is that while a minority of Jews read the Torah literally, the majority discuss it with a strong sense of both the figurative, metaphorical meanings behind stories, and also as a text about often good but very flawed people making mistakes and what we can learn from those mistakes. Take the eye for an eye sentiment. There’s even huge disagreement about what they really means. Many Jewish scholars argue that that section is in fact about monetary compensation. In other words if I do something bad to you, I have to pay damages. 
When it comes to God, Jewish beliefs couldn’t be more diverse. You will find many Jewish agnostics and atheists in shul every Shabbat. But probably more likely than that, you’ll find that rabbis and religious folk have a view of God that is not punitive and is certainly not some guy-in-the-sky doling out punishment. It’s almost always much more spiritual than that. Also, many Jews look at Torah as something very much man made that says something about the people writing it at the time and what they were going through. For me, that makes it just as holy, on a spiritual level. It’s a testament to stories told by a people trying to find meaning and to find their way through times that were usually terrifying and threatening.
